notes.definition: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. The power of a circuit device depends on the potential difference across it and the current through it: power = potential difference × current (P = V I), or, using V = I R, power = current² × resistance (P = I² R).
explanation: Every circuit device transfers energy. A kettle transfers energy to the water's thermal store, a motor to a kinetic store, a lamp to the surroundings by light and heating. The power of a device is how quickly it transfers energy: the energy transferred each second. Power is measured in watts (W), where 1 W is 1 joule per second, and large powers are given in kilowatts (1 kW = 1000 W).

The power transferred by a device depends on both the potential difference across it and the current through it. A larger potential difference means each coulomb of charge transfers more energy; a larger current means more coulombs pass each second. So power = potential difference × current, P = V I, with P in watts, V in volts and I in amperes. You must remember this equation.

If you know the current and the resistance instead of the potential difference, use power = (current)² × resistance, P = I² R. This comes from substituting V = I R into P = V I. Because the current is squared, doubling the current through a fixed resistor makes the power four times as large. This equation is useful for working out the energy wasted by heating in wires and cables.

To use these equations, convert to standard units first: kilowatts to watts (× 1000), milliamps to amps (÷ 1000) and kilohms to ohms (× 1000). Rearrange before substituting. From P = V I you get I = P ÷ V and V = P ÷ I. From P = I² R you get R = P ÷ I² and, for higher-level questions, I = √(P ÷ R).

Appliances are labelled with their power rating, for example a 2.3 kW kettle on a 230 V supply. From P = V I the current is I = 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A. Appliances that heat things, such as kettles, heaters and hair dryers, usually have the highest power ratings and draw the largest currents.
keyFacts: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W); 1 W = 1 J/s.
P = V I: power (W) = potential difference (V) × current (A).
P = I² R: power (W) = current² (A²) × resistance (Ω).
P = I² R comes from combining P = V I with V = I R.
Doubling the current through a fixed resistance quadruples the power.
Higher power appliances transfer energy faster and draw more current from the same supply.

keyTerms.definition: The rate at which energy is transferred, or the energy transferred per second.
The unit of power; 1 W is a transfer of 1 joule per second.
The power of an appliance when it is working normally, shown on its label.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, in volts.
Opposition to current, in ohms; a current through a resistance causes heating.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think doubling the current through a resistor doubles the power.
misconceptions.right: In fact P = I² R, so doubling the current makes the power four times as large.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget to square the current in P = I² R, or square the whole of I × R.
misconceptions.right: In fact only the current is squared: P = I × I × R.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think power and energy are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact power is the rate of energy transfer (joules per second); energy is measured in joules.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often substitute kilowatts directly into P = V I.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must convert kilowatts to watts (× 1000) first.

realWorld: Appliance labels give power ratings: a kettle might be 3 kW, a phone charger about 10 W, an LED bulb about 5 W.
Electric showers have high power ratings, so they need thick cables that can carry large currents safely.
Engineers use P = I² R to calculate how much energy is wasted heating cables, which is why the National Grid uses low currents.
higherTier: Rearranging P = I² R to find the current needs a square root: I = √(P ÷ R).
examTips: Choose the equation from the data: use P = V I if you have V and I; use P = I² R if you have I and R.
Square the current before multiplying by R, and write down the squared value to show your working.
Convert kW to W and mA to A before substituting.
When asked to explain the effect of changing current on power, use P = I² R and say the power changes by the square of the factor.
summary: Power is the rate of energy transfer, in watts.
Doubling current through a fixed resistance gives four times the power.
Convert kW to W, mA to A and kΩ to Ω first.

questions.question: Give the definition of power.
markScheme: 1 mark: the rate at which energy is transferred / energy transferred per second
questions.explanation: Power tells you how quickly energy is transferred, not how much.

questions.question: Write down the two equations for electrical power that you need to recall.
markScheme: 1 mark: P = V I (power = potential difference × current)
1 mark: P = I² R (power = current² × resistance)
questions.explanation: Both must be recalled; neither is on the equation sheet.

questions.question: Explain how the power of a device depends on the potential difference across it and the current through it.
markScheme: 1 mark: a larger potential difference means more energy is transferred by each coulomb of charge
1 mark: a larger current means more charge flows per second
1 mark: so power = potential difference × current
questions.explanation: Volts are joules per coulomb and amps are coulombs per second, so V × I gives joules per second.
acceptedAnswers: larger pd more energy per charge
larger current more charge per second

questions.question: Show how the equation P = I² R can be obtained from P = V I and V = I R.
markScheme: 1 mark: substitute V = I R into P = V I
1 mark: P = (I R) × I = I² R
questions.explanation: Replacing V with I R gives P = I × R × I = I² R.

questions.question: A student says that the current through a resistor is tripled, so the power is tripled. Explain why the student is wrong and state the correct factor.
markScheme: 1 mark: P = I² R, so power depends on the square of the current
1 mark: power increases by a factor of 9 (3²)
questions.explanation: Tripling I multiplies I² by 9, so the power is nine times as large (resistance assumed constant).

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the power ratings of some appliances that are connected to the 230 V mains supply.
Suggest why appliances that heat things, such as kettles and fan heaters, draw a larger current than the other appliances.
markScheme: 1 mark: they have a higher power rating
1 mark: the potential difference is the same (230 V), so I = P ÷ V is larger
questions.explanation: Heating needs a lot of energy quickly. At a fixed 230 V, a higher power means a higher current.

questions.question:
A student is given a 12 V power supply, an ammeter, a voltmeter and a small electric heater.
Describe how the student could find the power of the heater, and explain how they could use their results to calculate the resistance of the heater in two different ways.
markScheme: Indicative content: connect the heater in series with the ammeter and supply; connect the voltmeter in parallel across the heater; switch on and record V and I; calculate power using P = V I; resistance method 1: R = V ÷ I; resistance method 2: rearrange P = I² R to R = P ÷ I²; the two values should agree; switch off between readings because the heater gets hot (resistance changes with temperature); repeat and take a mean; safety: do not touch the heater element.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct circuit, correct power calculation and both methods for resistance clearly explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct circuit or power calculation with one method for resistance.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant points, such as measuring current or naming P = V I.
questions.explanation: Both resistance methods come from the same data: R = V ÷ I directly, or R = P ÷ I² using the calculated power.

questions.question:
Two heaters, A and B, are connected to the same 230 V supply. Heater A has twice the resistance of heater B.
Compare the currents through the heaters and the powers they transfer. Explain your answer using equations.
markScheme: Indicative content: same potential difference for both; I = V ÷ R, so A (twice the resistance) has half the current of B; P = V I, same V, so A has half the power of B; check with P = I² R: A has (½)² × 2 = ½ the power of B; so heater B (lower resistance) transfers energy faster and heats faster; numerical example, e.g. B = 23 Ω: I = 10 A, P = 2300 W; A = 46 Ω: I = 5 A, P = 1150 W.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct comparisons of both current and power with justification from equations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one correct comparison with limited justification.
questions.explanation: With the same potential difference, the lower-resistance heater draws more current and so transfers more power. Using P = I² R alone can mislead because both I and R change.

questions.question: Which of these appliances is likely to have the highest power rating?
questions.explanation: Heating appliances transfer a lot of energy quickly, so they have high power ratings (often 2 to 3 kW). The others are only a few watts.
